title: Daily Health Briefing
intro: Good morning! Here's today's research digest across your tracked topics, focused on fresh angles from the last few weeks — anti-aging devices & topicals (not just pills), body-composition and cycle-phase data for HIIT, three new pelvic-floor RCTs, updated HER2+/TP53 clinical data, and a supplement-by-supplement look at sleep aids. Reputable citations (PubMed, JAMA Network Open, ClinicalTrials.gov, AASM, dermatology & sleep journals) are linked as chips below each section. Informational only — not medical advice.

sections.body:
This week's theme: the field is broadening beyond "longevity pills" into **skin devices and topicals** that actually have controlled data — while the systemic-drug story stays cautious.

**Systemic drugs (still investigational).** A **2026 review of advanced anti-aging therapies** frames **rapamycin (mTOR inhibition)** as the front-runner, but notes the human PEARL trial's benefits were **modest and sex-specific** (mainly preserved *lean tissue mass in women*), partly because the compounded drug had only ~⅓ the bioavailability of commercial rapamycin. **NAD+ precursors** show small physical-performance gains; **senolytics** (dasatinib+quercetin, fisetin) remain early with inconsistent epigenetic-clock results. A new NIH-registered trial, **RESTOR (NCT06658093)**, launched **March 2026** to nail down *optimal intermittent mTOR-inhibitor dosing* separately in older women and men — a sign the field is still figuring out basic dosing. Bottom line: off-label longevity prescribing is running **ahead of the evidence**; no drug has shown human lifespan extension.

**Topicals — retinoids are still the gold standard.** A 2026 literature review reaffirms **topical tretinoin (0.025–0.1%)** improves fine/coarse wrinkles, pigmentation and sallowness, with histology showing **increased type I/III collagen** and down-regulated matrix metalloproteinases. Retinol/newer retinoid blends trade some potency for **better tolerability**.

**Devices — red/near-infrared LED is maturing.** A **12-week in-use study** of an at-home **LED face mask** (women 35–60, moderate photoageing, 10 min ×5/week) showed measurable **biomechanical gains** (improved elasticity/resilience by week 6). A broader photobiomodulation review confirms **consistent photoaging improvement** (texture, elasticity, fine-wrinkle reduction) with red/NIR light, while cautioning that **consumer devices deliver lower irradiance** than clinic systems and that visible light can worsen **melasma** in darker skin types (use photoprotection).

Practical framing: for proven "anti-aging," the highest-evidence, lowest-risk stack is still **daily sunscreen + a retinoid**, optionally augmented with **red-light therapy**; treat single-supplement longevity claims skeptically.

sections.body:
Fresh evidence sharpens *what* HIIT does for women — and *how to periodize it* around the cycle and menopause.

**Fat loss & body composition.** A large meta-analysis (**38 studies, 959 women**) found HIIT significantly reduces **body weight, total fat, and abdominal fat** — but with important nuance: effects on weight/total/abdominal fat were **statistically significant mainly *before* menopause**, and **cycling-based HIIT outperformed running**, especially in postmenopausal women. Programs **≥8 weeks, ~3 sessions/week** were most efficient. So postmenopausal women shouldn't expect the same scale-weight drop from HIIT alone — pair it with resistance training and nutrition.

**Cardiometabolic markers.** A separate meta-analysis in postmenopausal women found HIIT specifically **lowered glucose, triglycerides, total cholesterol and LDL** (where slower "speed interval" work did not) — a solid case for HIIT as a metabolic tool even when the scale barely moves.

**Cycle-phase periodization (new).** The **FENDURA project** measured VO2, HR, ventilation, lactate and perceived exertion across the menstrual cycle during standardized HIIT (5×4-min at 80%). Group-level differences were **minor** — meaning most women *don't* need to overhaul training by phase. But a cyclist RCT found **24-hour recovery was impaired in the late-luteal phase**. Practical read: keep the plan consistent, but if **luteal-phase** sessions feel disproportionately hard (higher core temp raises perceived effort), individualize — **add 10–15 s of rest per interval, drop the last interval, or go lower-impact** — rather than forcing the same session.

sections.body:
Three **new 2026 randomized trials** all reinforce that **pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT)** is effective first-line care — and show how to boost it.

- **Add-on hormone (postmenopausal SUI).** A **2026 RCT** (*Canadian Journal of Urology*) found **vaginal androgen + PFMT** improved stress-incontinence remission **more than PFMT alone** in postmenopausal women — a plausible synergy given estrogen/androgen effects on the urogenital tissues. Discuss with a urogynecologist; topical hormones aren't for everyone.
- **Structured, supervised programs work.** A **12-week nurse-led PFMT RCT** (120 postmenopausal women) cut incontinence severity dramatically (ICIQ-UI SF 7.7 vs 13.7 in controls; Cohen's *d* ≈ 1.7) and **raised pelvic-floor strength**, with benefits **sustained at 6 months** across stress, mixed and urge subtypes — evidence that *coached* programs beat "just do Kegels."
- **Prehab before surgery.** In women with SUI **awaiting sling surgery**, **6 weeks of intensive preoperative PFMT** significantly improved muscle strength and symptom severity — and **43% postponed their planned operation** afterward. Low-risk, low-cost, and it can defer surgery for many.

Key point unchanged: **technique and consistency beat rep-counting.** Confirm you're activating the right muscles (a clinician or biofeedback helps), and favor supervised or structured programs.

sections.body:
For **HER2-positive, TP53/p53-mutated** breast cancer, the most relevant recent work explains *why* these "co-mutated" tumors resist standard targeted drugs — and how to turn that against them.

- A mechanistic study (now in **PMC / peer review, 2025**) bred **HER2 + TP53 co-mutant** mouse models. These tumors grew faster and were **resistant to neratinib alone**, but showed **increased histone acetylation, open chromatin and hyper-transcription of DNA-repair genes** — which made them **sensitive to the topoisomerase-I (TOP1) inhibitor payload (exatecan/deruxtecan)** in **trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd / Enhertu)**. Combining **neratinib + T-DXd** was highly effective preclinically. This vulnerability depended on the *transcriptional activity* of the p53 mutations — a rational, biomarker-driven strategy.
- That combination is being tested in a **phase 1 multi-institution trial (NCI ETCTN 10495, NCT05372614)** in HER2-altered solid tumors.
- On the **standard-of-care** front, the **final analysis of DESTINY-Breast07** (presented at **ASCO 2026**) reported first-line **T-DXd ± durvalumab** data in HER2+ metastatic breast cancer — reinforcing T-DXd's central, expanding role in HER2+ disease.

Important framing: this is **early-stage, investigational** science. "Alternative" here should mean **evidence-based options discussed with an oncologist**, *not* a substitute for standard care. p53 itself remains largely **"undruggable"** — there is still **no approved p53-targeted therapy** — so exploiting p53's *downstream* vulnerabilities (like TOP1 sensitivity) is the pragmatic path.

sections.body:
You asked specifically about **supplements** for restless/disjointed sleep, so here's a supplement-by-supplement, evidence-graded look — followed by the behavioral baseline.

**What the supplement data actually show:**

1. **Magnesium (bisglycinate/glycinate) — moderate.** A **2025 randomized, placebo-controlled trial** (155 adults with poor sleep) found **250 mg elemental magnesium bisglycinate (+ glycine) for 4 weeks** produced a **small but statistically significant** drop in Insomnia Severity Index (effect size *d* ≈ 0.2), mostly within the first 14 days, and was **well tolerated**. Reasonable, low-risk option for mild insomnia; don't expect a dramatic effect.
2. **L-theanine — moderate (best for stress-driven restlessness).** A **2025 meta-analysis (19 RCTs, N≈897)** found subjective sleep improvements; it promotes calm "alpha" brain activity. Typical dose **200 mg** before bed. Works on *arousal/anxiety*, not circadian timing.
3. **Glycine (~3 g) — plausible, low-risk.** Often paired with magnesium; small trials suggest faster sleep onset and better subjective quality.
4. **Melatonin — strong, but only for *timing*.** Best for **jet lag, shift work, delayed sleep phase**; **low doses (0.3–1 mg)** are preferred. Not a great fit for chronic "can't-stay-asleep" insomnia, where guidelines lean *against* routine use.
5. **Apigenin / chamomile — weak.** No RCTs of isolated apigenin; chamomile trials were largely non-significant.

**The behavioral baseline still wins.** The **2026 AASM combination-therapy guideline** analyzed 15 RCTs and found a clear asymmetry: **adding CBT-I to medication helps**, but **adding medication to CBT-I adds little** (and may nudge daytime mood worse). **CBT-I remains first-line** for chronic insomnia.

**Habits for restless/disjointed sleep:** fixed **wake time** (even weekends); bed for **sleep only**; cool, dark, quiet room; dim lights / cut screens during a wind-down window; and if problems persist beyond a few weeks, see a provider to rule out **sleep apnea** and consider **CBT-I** (digital programs work too).
